did_you_know.text: The high priest Eliashib and his fellow priests began the restoration work: they built the Sheep Gate, consecrated it, and set its doors in place as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel.
The people of Tekoa took part in the building, but the nobles of Tekoa did not join the work; the text notes that they would not put their necks to the work of their Lord.
The people of Gibeon and the men of Mizpah also helped build the wall, along with groups who came from Jerusalem and other settlements.

Among the builders were skilled craftsmen: Uzziel son of Harhaiah belonged to the goldsmiths, and Hananiah son of the perfumers belonged to the apothecaries. Their work extended as far as the Broad Wall.
Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, worked on the building together with his daughters; this is an explicit mention of his daughters as partners in the effort.
Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah built the Valley Gate, and they also set its doors, bolts, and bars in place. The section they built extended for a thousand cubits as far as the Dung Gate.
Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, worked on a section of the wall as far as the area opposite the tombs of David, the artificial pool, and the House of the Mighty.
The Levites and the district rulers took part in the building, and in several places the text notes that the workers undertook a “second measure”—that is, an additional section of work.
The people of Tekoa, who had already been mentioned at the beginning of the chapter, worked on another section of the wall, opposite the great projecting tower and as far as the wall of Ophel.
Despite Sanballat and Tobiah’s mockery, the wall was joined together up to half its height, and the text concludes that the people had the heart and determination to continue the work.
